source.title: Big Transfer (BiT): General Visual Representation Learning
source.authors: Alexander Kolesnikov; Lucas Beyer; Xiao-Hua Zhai; J. Puigcerver; Jessica Yung; S. Gelly; N. Houlsby

page_placements.theme: Model capacity, data and training must scale jointly

record.file_problem: No material file problem; the full paper and supplementary sections are present, though some figure and table formatting is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: It reports visual downstream performance after varying pretraining data and model scale, extending the downstream-performance scaling question to vision. It does not test language-model pretraining loss laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and says a similar model-size/data-size interaction appears in language modelling, but that cited result is not this study’s evidence. The paper does not fit power laws or report held-out pretraining loss. Its own visual scaling results bear on downstream performance versus scale (V6), but not on the power-law form, loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: The study is a recipe paper for supervised visual transfer, BiT, using ResNets. Its scale analysis varies architecture (R50x1 to R152x4) and upstream dataset (1.3M, 14M, 300M images) and reports downstream accuracy. It fits no power law and reports no held-out pretraining loss, so it cannot bear on V1, V2, V3, V5 or V7. It extrapolates nothing. Its systems are vision classifiers, not language models, so its accuracy-versus-scale results do not measure V6 for the kind of system V6 names. V5 covers other modalities, but only for the power-law form, which the study never tests. The study cites Kaplan et al. as showing a similar model-size/data-size interaction, so it discusses the claim without testing any version. The reader's T3/tests/V6 assignment is not adopted. The results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right, but incomplete. The paper's main conclusion is that a simple recipe gives strong generalist transfer across many datasets and data regimes, including few-shot. That recipe is large-scale supervised pretraining with GroupNorm plus Weight Standardization and the BiT-HyperRule fine-tuning heuristic. In the scale analysis, the authors conclude that model size and upstream data must grow together, with enough training compute. Scaling only one can give limited or negative benefit. They propose no scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: Supervised visual pretraining with ResNet models and evaluation of downstream accuracy; no language-model cross-entropy loss, power-law fitting, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported visual scaling effect depends on the combination of model size and pretraining dataset size; the paper notes that scaling only one may fail to improve downstream performance.

fits_no_version.finding: In supervised vision pretraining and transfer, downstream accuracy rises when model size and upstream data grow together. Growing only one gives limited gains, and sometimes losses: R50x1 pretrained on JFT-300M can do worse than on ImageNet-21k (Fig. 5, Sec. 4.1). BiT-M beats BiT-S on all six benchmarks (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision transfer accuracy depends jointly on model capacity and pretraining data size. Scaling one alone can saturate or reverse.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed compute budget, the 'standard' ILSVRC-2012 budget (~100M images seen), pretraining on the larger ImageNet-21k gives worse ILSVRC-2012 accuracy. Only 3x or 10x longer training realises the benefit (Fig. 7 left). In vision, the gain from more data depends on compute, but no loss is measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains from larger pretraining datasets in vision require proportionally more training compute.

fits_no_version.finding: On ObjectNet, Table 6 gives numbers. Top-1 (resize & crop) for R152x4 is 36.0 (BiT-S), 47.0 (BiT-M) and 58.7 (BiT-L). R50x1 on JFT gives 37.6 versus 35.0 on ImageNet-21k, so the Fig. 5 reversal does not hold there. Accuracy is not monotone in architecture: BiT-L R101x1 scores 54.6 and R50x3 49.1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The direction of data-scale effects on vision transfer varies with the downstream task.

record.problems: The scaling results concern visual downstream accuracy, not held-out language-model loss. The figure-based comparison in r7 has no numeric values stated in the text. The reported scale comparisons do not establish a power law or prediction across several orders of magnitude.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 contains additional combinations of model architecture, upstream dataset, and downstream benchmark. They are not separately transcribed; r7 captures the text-explicit exception relevant to the tested version. Other results concern transfer performance or training components without testing the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss and no power-law fit.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No fixed-compute allocation analysis. 'Increase both in tandem' is qualitative only.
Architectures vary in size, not in shape at fixed parameter count.
Vision setting, but no test of power-law form.
No language-model downstream results and no relation to pretraining loss. Vision accuracy is given at 3 data scales and 5 sizes with no predictive fit.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Numeric ObjectNet top-1/top-5 accuracy across 5 architectures × 3 upstream datasets; the full model-by-data grid that no row records.
COCO detection AP by upstream data with fixed R101x3: 41.7 (ILSVRC-2012), 43.2 (ImageNet-21k), 43.8 (JFT-300M).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are dropped. The study fits no trend, measures no loss, and studies vision classifiers rather than language models. Its scale comparisons also confound data size with training schedule: BiT-L trains 40 epochs and the others 90. The Kaplan et al. citation is a cited result, not this study's evidence. If the project later treats vision downstream accuracy under V5 or V6, rows r1–r6 would show monotone improvement with data at R152x4, and r7 a data-scale reversal for R50x1. Even then, none of these rows shows a power-law form or predictability.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model loss or power-law fit is measured.
No predictions from smaller runs are compared with larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens is tested.
Architectures are varied, but not at fixed parameter count to measure changes in loss.
The study concerns vision, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in image models or other training regimes.
It measures visual downstream accuracy across pretraining scales, not language-model downstream performance or its relation to pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, or sensitivity to power-law fitting choices are examined.

relation.reason: Sections 2.1 and 4.1 discuss related scaling findings and cite Kaplan et al.; the study does not fit or test a scaling law.

tranche.reason: The study measures supervised visual transfer accuracy and qualitative interactions between model and dataset size; it neither tests nor uses the specified power-law or predictive scaling relationships.

source_check.notes: V6 is not explicitly restricted to language models, contrary to the pack's rationale. The exclusion remains justified because these results establish transfer trends without testing a predictive scaling relationship.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: BiT-M versus BiT-S on the six downstream benchmarks in Table 2
reader_labels.reason: With the same stated architecture and a larger pretraining dataset, BiT-M scores higher on all six reported downstream measures (r1–r6). This supports improvement in these tested conditions, not a power-law prediction.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ResNet-50x1 pretrained on JFT-300M versus ImageNet-21k
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that more pretraining data can reduce downstream performance for this architecture, so the direction of the scale effect is not uniform across model/data combinations (r7).
